resident.chief_complaint: Pain in the ulnar side of both arms since October 2006; clumsiness in both hands and disturbed gait since February 2007.
resident.history: The patient is a 58-year-old male carpenter. He first noticed pain in the ulnar side of both arms in October 2006 and had no history of trauma in the cervical or upper thoracic regions. Since February 2007, he experienced clumsiness in both hands and gait disturbance. He presented to the clinic on May 30. He reported pollakiuria. No other past medical history is documented.
resident.physical_exam: Gait was slightly spastic. Neurological examination revealed muscle weakness grade G in the bilateral wrist flexors, finger extensors, and iliopsoas muscles and grade F in the bilateral finger abductors. The triceps tendon reflex was decreased, while the knee and ankle jerks were accelerated bilaterally. Sensory disturbance was detected on the ulnar side of both arms, on the C8 dermatome, and on and below the L1 dermatomes. The Japanese Orthopaedic Association score for cervical myelopathy was 8 of 17. No laboratory values are documented in the record.

Spinal cord swelling and T2 hyperintensity at C7/T1 on MRI
Posterior cord compression at C7/T1 on paramedian MRI
Triangular deformity of the spinal cord and surface irregularity of facet joints on axial MRI
Complete block of contrast medium at C7/T1 on myelogram
Severe arthrosis with right-dominant bony spur formation from bilateral C7/T1 facet joints growing into spinal canal on CT myelography
resident.past_history: No history of trauma in the cervical and upper thoracic regions. Occupation: carpenter. Other past medical history is not documented.
resident.public_message: A 58-year-old male carpenter presented with pain in the ulnar side of both arms since October 2006, followed by clumsiness in both hands and gait disturbance since February 2007. Examination showed slightly spastic gait, pollakiuria, weakness grade G in bilateral wrist flexors, finger extensors, and iliopsoas, grade F in bilateral finger abductors, decreased triceps reflex, hyperactive knee and ankle reflexes, and sensory disturbance on the ulnar side of both arms, C8 dermatome, and L1 and below. JOA score was 8/17. Imaging revealed nonunion of the T1 spinous process fracture, slight anterolisthesis of C7, spinal cord swelling and T2 hyperintensity at C7/T1, posterior cord compression on paramedian MRI, triangular cord deformity, complete myelographic block at C7/T1, and severe facet joint arthrosis with right-dominant bony spur formation. No laboratory values are documented.

imaging.public_message: Reporting the case record's description of the imaging; the films were not available for review. At C7-T1, bilateral facet arthrosis with bony spur formation, right greater than left, extends into the spinal canal and produces posterior (dorsal) cord compression with anteroposterior cord deformity and complete myelographic block. The record describes slight T2 hyperintensity with cord swelling, consistent with equivocal cord T2 signal change. These findings correlate highly with the reported myelopathy.

neurology.localization: The findings localize primarily to the cervical spinal cord at the C7/T1 level, with segmental involvement of C7-T1 (weakness in wrist flexors, finger extensors, finger abductors, decreased triceps reflex) and corticospinal tract dysfunction causing spastic gait, hyperreflexia at knees/ankles, and lower limb weakness. The L1 sensory level is lower than expected for this lesion and remains unexplained, suggesting possible additional caudal cord involvement not demonstrated on provided imaging.

red_flags.finding: Sensory disturbance reported on and below the L1 dermatomes.
red_flags.rationale: A sensory level at L1 is many segments below the C7/T1 compression and is not explained by the localized cervical lesion. While it does not offer an alternative explanation for the upper limb and myelopathic signs, it warrants thoracic spine imaging to exclude an additional cord lesion before planning surgery.
Urinary frequency can occur with myelopathy but is nonspecific and may be urologic. It does not alter the localization or the surgical indication.

red_flags.finding: Nonunion of T1 spinous process fracture and slight anterolisthesis of C7.
red_flags.rationale: These findings may reflect prior trauma or mechanical changes, but the cord compression is attributed to facet joint arthrosis. They do not change the indication or the planned approach.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: Sensory level at L1 is lower than expected for the C7/T1 cord lesion and is not explained by the imaged compression.
neurology.public_message: Localization is cervical myelopathy at C7/T1 with segmental C7-T1 dysfunction and long tract signs. Imaging explains the myelopathic syndrome but not the L1 sensory level, so match is medium. Red flags: L1 sensory level (changes_plan; recommend thoracic imaging before surgical planning), pollakiuria (coexisting), nonunion T1 and C7 anterolisthesis (coexisting).

anesthesia.public_message: ASA grade III; intraoperative MAP target 85 mmHg; expected blood loss risk moderate; prone position tolerance high; extubation difficulty unassessable due to absent airway assessment.

preconditions_for_failure: No improvement in JOA score by at least 2 points after 3 months of structured conservative therapy
Worsening of gait or upper limb function during the trial
Development of new bowel or bladder dysfunction
Intolerance or inability to comply with prescribed physical therapy
Progression of cord signal change or increase in compression on repeat MRI
physiatrist_opening.public_message: Conservative management remains a defensible initial option, but this patient's severe imaging (complete myelographic block, cord T2 hyperintensity) and progressive myelopathy significantly reduce the expected benefit. I propose a strictly supervised 3-month trial of physical therapy, posture management, and fall prevention with close neurological monitoring, acknowledging a realistic success rate of about 20%. I also recognize the evidence against prolonged delay: with progressive symptoms and cord signal change, surgery is often performed to prevent irreversible deterioration. Therefore, failure to achieve meaningful improvement by these strict criteria should trigger prompt surgical referral.

The risk of irreversible deterioration is precisely why I propose only a 3-month, closely monitored trial rather than indefinite conservative management. I maintain my position.

vice_opinions.assessment: This patient has progressive cervical myelopathy (JOA 8/17) caused by C7/T1 facet arthrosis with dorsal bony spur compressing the cord, complete myelographic block, and T2 cord signal change. There is also C7 anterolisthesis and T1 spinous process nonunion suggesting segmental instability. The L1 sensory level is unexplained by cervical imaging and warrants thoracic evaluation before surgical planning. Given severe compression and progressive deficit, surgical decompression is indicated, but timing and approach need director's determination. Conservative trial of 3 months carries risk of irreversible deterioration; I lean toward early surgery after obtaining thoracic MRI.
proposed_options: Proceed with surgical decompression and instrumented fusion at C7-T1 (posterior approach likely) as soon as thoracic MRI rules out a separate lesion; treat pollakiuria symptomatically.
Institute a strictly supervised 3-month conservative trial (per physiatrist) with close neurologic monitoring; proceed to surgery if no improvement or progression.
First complete diagnostic workup: thoracic MRI (and possibly lumbar) to explain L1 sensory level, urology evaluation for pollakiuria; then decide on surgery.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Option 1: early surgical decompression and fusion after thoracic MRI, because the severity of compression and cord signal change outweigh the limited benefit of conservative care.
disagreement_points: Whether the L1 sensory level requires full thoracic MRI before surgery or can be deferred to postoperative workup if surgery is urgent.
Whether a 3-month conservative trial is justifiable given complete myelographic block and cord T2 signal change, or whether it risks irreversible neurologic loss.
Surgical approach and extent of fusion: posterior-only decompression/fusion versus combined anterior-posterior given the dorsal compression and C7 anterolisthesis.
Need for urologic evaluation of pollakiuria before surgery or as part of postoperative management.
deferred_questions_to_director: Do you agree that we should proceed with surgery now, or would you support a short monitored conservative trial?
Should we obtain thoracic MRI before scheduling surgery, or can we proceed if there is no clinical evidence of thoracic cord lesion?
What surgical approach and fusion levels do you favor for this C7/T1 dorsal compression with C7 anterolisthesis and T1 spinous nonunion?
vice_opinions.public_message: Director, I agree this is progressive C7/T1 myelopathy from posterior bony compression with complete block and cord signal change. I favor proceeding to surgical decompression and fusion, but the L1 sensory level is unexplained and should prompt thoracic MRI before we finalize. I would not support a 3-month conservative trial given the high risk of irreversible deterioration. My main contested questions are the timing and surgical approach: posterior-only versus combined, and whether we require thoracic imaging first. I defer the final decision to you.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is progressive C7/T1 myelopathy with complete myelographic block, cord signal change, and instability features (C7 anterolisthesis, T1 spinous process nonunion). Surgical decompression and fusion is indicated; I support the director's plan to obtain thoracic MRI before finalizing. I do not support conservative management. The main unresolved issues are surgical approach and fusion extent.
proposed_options: Urgent thoracic MRI, then posterior decompression and instrumented fusion at C7-T1, extending to C6 and/or T2 as needed for instability.
If MRI shows ventral compression from the right-dominant spur that cannot be adequately addressed posteriorly, add a staged anterior approach for direct decompression and interbody fusion.
Brief observation during imaging workup only if thoracic MRI is delayed, but no more than 48-72 hours.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior decompression and fusion at C7-T1 with extension to C6 or T2 as needed, after thoracic MRI.
disagreement_points: Posterior-only versus combined anterior-posterior approach for the right-dominant ventral bony spur.
Whether to preemptively extend fusion to C6 and T2 given the C7 anterolisthesis and T1 spinous process nonunion, or to limit to C7-T1 and extend only if intraoperative instability is demonstrated.
The exact urgency: should the thoracic MRI and surgery be completed within 48-72 hours, or is a few days of observation acceptable while imaging and urologic evaluation proceed?
deferred_questions_to_director: Do you agree with scheduling thoracic MRI within 24-48 hours and surgery immediately thereafter if no additional lesion is found?
What is your threshold for adding an anterior decompression if the posterior approach does not fully resolve the ventral cord compression?
Should the fusion construct routinely include C6 and T2, or be decided intraoperatively based on instability after decompression?

My preferred plan is posterior decompression and instrumented fusion at C7-T1, extending to C6 or T2 if imaging or intraoperative findings show instability. The main contested points I want settled are whether the right-dominant ventral spur requires an added anterior approach and whether we should preemptively extend the fusion. I also want your decision on timing: I favor thoracic MRI within 24-48 hours, with surgery immediately after if no additional lesion appears. I defer the final approach and construct to your judgement.

director_rulings.public_message: I agree with the Deputy Director that this patient has progressive C7/T1 myelopathy with complete myelographic block and cord signal change; surgery is indicated as things stand, and I do not support a 3-month conservative trial given the risk of irreversible deterioration. However, the unexplained L1 sensory level raised by Neurology warrants a thoracic MRI before we finalize the surgical plan. Dr. Resident, please give your specific view on the urgency: would you schedule the thoracic MRI and then surgery within days, or do you see any reason for a brief observation during the imaging workup? Dr. Radiologist, please specify the thoracic MRI protocol and whether the cervical findings suggest any additional upper thoracic abnormalities that might alter the operative approach. Contingency: If thoracic MRI shows no additional lesion, we will proceed to early posterior decompression and fusion at C7-T1 (with extension as needed for the C7 anterolisthesis). If it shows an additional compressive or signal abnormality, we will bring the case back to adjust the plan before operating. We will also obtain urologic evaluation for the pollakiuria as part of preoperative assessment.

director_rulings.final_decision: We will obtain a thoracic MRI within 24-48 hours to evaluate the unexplained L1 sensory level before finalizing the surgical plan. If the MRI shows no additional lesion, we will proceed to posterior decompression and instrumented fusion at C7-T1, with extension to C6 or T2 only if intraoperative instability is demonstrated or if the C7 anterolisthesis/T1 nonunion requires stabilization. The threshold for adding an anterior decompression is persistent ventral cord compression after posterior decompression (assessed intraoperatively or on postoperative imaging) or a right-dominant bony spur occupying more than one-third of the spinal canal diameter on preoperative CT. If the MRI reveals an additional compressive or signal abnormality, we will reconvene before operating.
